_note: NT verses that declare a reference, and the OT passage Flash reads each as pointing to (tools/meaning/declared_refs.py). A reading, credited; 'other' is Flash's own suggestion, a lower claim.

reason: “Just as I directed the churches of Galatia” is Paul's own prior instruction, not an Old Testament citation.
“Not to go beyond what is written” is a maxim, not a citation of any specific OT passage; no candidate matches.
“Must walk as Jesus walked” compares believers to Christ, not to an Old Testament text.
Lev 20:26 in context reads “You are to be holy to Me because I, the LORD, am holy,” the closest match to “Be holy, because I am holy.”
“Being examples to the flock” and “not lording it over” echo Ezek 34 and shepherd imagery, but no candidate is a citation.
Paul calls the Thessalonians an example/type for believers; no OT passage is cited or echoed, the candidates being general 'remembrance/sign' texts.
'Just as ... so' here is the comparative structure within the sentence (approved by God / not pleasing men), not a citation of an OT text.
Timothy is told to become a 'type' (example) for believers; no OT passage stands behind the word, and the youth texts listed are not cited.
The 'just as ... so' is Paul's own comparison between Christ's sufferings and comfort; no OT passage is quoted, despite the psalm/comfort language.
Paul's readiness to punish disobedience is not a fulfilment citation; the vengeance texts listed are not being quoted.
Paul's 'just as much as he does' compares his standing in Christ to the rival's, not citing any OT passage.
Paul quotes 'I believed, therefore I have spoken' from LXX Ps 115:1 (MT 116:10); none of the candidates match.
'Just as he had started it' points back to Titus's earlier work in Corinth, not to the OT.
Paul offers himself as a 'type'/example (cf. 1 Thess 1:6-7; 2 Thess 3:7), echoing apostolic example rather than a specific OT text; none of the candidates fit.
Recalling Timothy's tears is personal, not a citation of an OT passage; the Hezekiah parallels are verbal coincidence.
Peter quotes "he who shared my bread has lifted up his heel against me," which is Ps 41:9; the listed candidates are word-search noise about Judah.
Paul speaks generally of all that was written about Him (cf. Luke 24:44-46), not a specific OT passage, and none of the candidates fits.
James cites "I will rebuild the fallen tent of David" (quoted in vv.16-17), which is Amos 9:11-12; all candidates are Chronicles 'written in the records' noise.
Paul's travel plan contains no citation or comparison to Scripture, and none of the candidates relates to it.
This is the narrator introducing Claudius Lysias's own letter; it cites no OT passage, and the 'a type' label here reflects a similarity to letter-introductions, not a citation.
A general claim to believe 'the Law and the Prophets', not a citation of any specific OT passage.
Narrative summary of Felix leaving Paul imprisoned; the 'fulfilled' tag is spurious and no OT text is referenced.
Stephen narrates the angel in the flame of the burning bush, the Exodus 3 Sinai/Horeb theophany.
The preceding verse explicitly quotes 'the book of the prophets' (Amos), and 7:43 continues that citation.
The 'pattern he had seen' echoes the command to build the tabernacle according to the pattern shown Moses (cf. Exod 25:40; Num 8:4).
This is Paul's own prayer report, not a citation of or allusion to any Old Testament passage; the candidates are keyword matches on 'wisdom'/'will' with no textual link.
The 'just as' compares believers' forgiveness to the Lord's forgiveness of them (Christ), not to any Old Testament text.
No citation formula; the 'fullness of God' language is Paul's own, and the candidates match only on the word 'love'.
Paul quotes 'Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law,' which is Deuteronomy 27:26, not any listed candidate.
Paul quotes 'Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree,' which is Deuteronomy 21:23, candidate 1.
Paul's two sons of Abraham (slave woman/free woman) restates the Genesis 21:10 account of Sarah, Hagar and Ishmael.
Hagar and Mount Sinai are allegorised from the Hagar narrative in Genesis 16, not from any of the listed Sinai-tablet passages.
The persecution of the son born by the Spirit refers to Ishmael mocking Isaac in Genesis 21:9.
Psalm 40:7 contains the exact words 'Then I said, Here I am, I have come— it is written about me in the scroll.'
The offering for his own sins and the people's sins echoes the Aaron/Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16:15, but the verse's comparison is really to Aaron's calling.
This is an analogy comparing body/spirit to faith/deeds, not a citation of any OT passage.
The quoted words 'Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion... seated on the colt of a donkey' are from Zechariah 9:9, which is not among the candidates.
The verse refers back to the same Scripture just quoted in 12:14-15, Zechariah 9:9, not any listed candidate.
John 12:3 is a narrative anointing scene with no stated citation of an OT passage.
This is Jesus speaking about the Father's command, not citing or comparing to an OT passage.
"Just as ... so" here expresses Jesus' own obedience to the Father's command, not a citation of an OT text; no candidate matches.
The verse states the purpose of Jesus' own words ("I have told you these things"), not a fulfilment or citation of any OT passage.
"They hated Me without reason" is the citation of Ps 69:4 (69:5 MT), quoted explicitly as "written in their Law"; no candidate matches.
The vine/branch imagery is Jesus' own metaphor for remaining in Him; "just as ... so" compares, it does not cite an OT passage.
The Scripture "fulfilled" by the son of destruction is the betrayal text of Ps 41:9 (cf. Jn 13:18); no candidate matches, and the reference is not named in the verse.
It fulfills a word Jesus Himself had spoken (cf. Jhn 12:32-33), not an OT passage; the word-search candidates are irrelvant.
The words fulfilled are Jesus' own, spoken in Jhn 17:12, not an OT citation.
The 'it is written' here describes the placard actually written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek, not a citation of Scripture.
Same placard, literally written in three languages; no OT passage is being pointed to.
Thomas' demand to see and touch is a condition of belief, not a typological citation of any OT text.
The verse refers to signs not written 'in this book', i.e. John's own gospel, with no citation of an OT passage.
The clause is about the purpose of writing this gospel, not a citation of an OT text; 'it is written' is a spurious tag.
Jesus explicitly names Moses lifting up the snake in the wilderness, which is Num 21:9.
The 'just as ... so' compares the Father's and the Son's giving of life within the Godhead; no OT passage is cited or alluded to.
The 'as ... so' compares the Father's self-existent life with the Son's granted life, an internal Trinitarian statement with no OT citation.
The two-witness rule is stated in the Law (Deut 19:15; cf. Num 35:30; Deut 17:6), which none of the word-search candidates is.

Gabriel's words are about his own message being fulfilled in time; the clause 'as it is written' / citation formula is absent and no OT passage is in view, so the candidates (Ezek, Joel, Kings, Chronicles, Joshua, Jeremiah) are incidental matches.

Jesus asks a general question about what the Law says; the answer he draws out is Deut 6:5 and Lev 19:18, but the verse itself cites no specific passage, so none of the candidates (Deut 28:58 etc.) is what it 'points to'.
The sign of Jonah is the prophet's preaching to Nineveh; candidate 6 (Jonah 1:1) is the call of Jonah, not the sign, so the passage pointed to is Jonah's ministry to Nineveh.
This is a comparison (lightning lighting the sky) with no citation of or allusion to a text; the candidates are only verbal echoes ('one end ... the other').
The 'days of Noah' (eating, drinking, marrying, the flood) come from the Genesis flood narrative, especially Gen 6-7, not any candidate passage.
It refers generically to 'the prophets' as a whole, not to any specific written passage a candidate names.
'Days of vengeance' evokes the Song of Moses (Deut 32:35, 'vengeance is Mine'), but Luke may only allude generally; none of the candidates fit.
Jerusalem trodden down and 'times of the Gentiles' echo Daniel's seventy-weeks prophecy of the city's desolation.
This is Jesus' own statement about the Passover's fulfillment in the kingdom, not a citation of a specific OT passage.
This is the disciples reporting their own visit to the tomb, not citing or comparing to any Old Testament passage.
Jesus summarises 'the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms' as a whole, not one passage; no candidate fits and no single reference can be named.
The suffering-and-rising-on-the-third-day summary is drawn from Isaiah (esp. 53) and Hosea 6:2; no candidate matches.
The quoted line 'The Spirit of the Lord is on Me...' is Isaiah 61:1, which none of the candidates give (they are only word-search hits on 'find/found').
The quoted prophecy 'the virgin will be with child... Immanuel' is Isaiah 7:14; the candidates are irrelevant matches on 'prophet'.
The quoted words 'Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen... I will put My Spirit on Him' are Isaiah 42:1, none of the candidates (all narrative mentions of the prophet Isaiah).
Jonah 1:17 states Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights, exactly the comparison Jesus draws.
This is the interpretation of Jesus' own parable of the weeds (Matt 13:24-30), an analogy within the parable, not a citation of an Old Testament passage.
Part of the parable of the dragnet (Matt 13:47-50); it is Jesus' own similitude and cites no Old Testament text.
The quotation 'A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children' is Jeremiah 31:15, none of the listed candidates (all narrative mentions of Jeremiah).
No listed candidate is cited; the saying is not a verbatim quotation but a targum-like wordplay on Hebrew neṣer ('branch', Isa 11:1), so the referent is uncertain.
The quoted words 'But you, Bethlehem... out of you will come a ruler' are Micah 5:2; none of the candidates match it.
The quote 'Say to the Daughter of Zion, see your King comes, gentle and riding on a donkey' is Zechariah 9:9; no candidate contains it.
The lightning-east-to-west clause is a simile for the visibility of the coming, not a citation of any OT passage.
'As it was in the days of Noah' refers to the flood narrative in Genesis 6-7; the nearest candidate Gen 6:4 concerns the Nephilim rather than the days' corruption.

The phrase 'it is written about Him' is a general reference to Scripture's testimony of the suffering Son of Man (cf. Isa 53; Ps 22) and no candidate matches; the 'woe' echoes general judgment oracles.
General statement that the Scriptures must be fulfilled in the passion; no specific OT passage or candidate corresponds.
Collective reference to 'the writings of the prophets' being fulfilled, with no single passage or candidate identified.
This is the Roman titulus/inscription on the cross, not a citation of Scripture; the 'it is written' note refers to the posted charge itself.
Matthew quotes 'they took the thirty pieces of silver...potter's field,' which is Zechariah 11:12-13, though he attributes it to Jeremiah.
The quoted 'Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali... Galilee of the Gentiles' is Isaiah 9:1-2, not any candidate (all of which introduce Isaiah only as a prophet).
The 'one who dips his hand into the bowl with Me' betrayal is generally read against Psalm 41:9 ('he who shared my bread has lifted up his heel'), which is not among the candidates.
The phrase is a general appeal to 'the Scriptures' being fulfilled with no specific Old Testament passage named; none of the candidates is a citation.
The suffering and rejection of the Son of Man is most likely Isaiah 53, and it is not among the candidates, but I am not certain a single passage is in view.
What was 'written about' Elijah being done to him likely refers to the hostility against Elijah in 1 Kings, but I cannot pin the exact passage and none of the candidates fits.
Paul points to his own apostolic example, not to an Old Testament text; no citation formula is present.
“what is written in it” refers to this prophecy book itself, not to an Old Testament passage.
The “written” is the Lamb's Book of Life; no Old Testament passage is cited.
The “written” is the name on the foreheads of the 144,000; no Old Testament text is cited.
The “written” is the name on the woman's forehead; the allusions to Babylon and Ezek 9:4 are echoes, not a citation.

The 'was, and is not, and yet will be' wording and 'Book of Life' are John's own apocalyptic formulae with no single OT citation; the listed candidates (deep/abyss, writing) are only verbal parallels.
The rider's fiery/white imagery and the enthroned figure echo Daniel's Ancient of Days vision (Dan 7:9), and Dan 7 is the chapter behind Rev 19's Son of Man imagery.
The title 'KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS' written on robe and thigh has no OT citation; the candidates (thigh, kings of Persia) are coincidence word-matches.
The 'hidden manna' alludes to the jar of manna preserved before the LORD (Exod 16:33), not merely the manna given in Exod 16:15.
The open books and judgment of the dead echo Dan 7:10 ('the books were opened'), but that reference is not among the candidates, and the 'Book of Life' phrase is John's own.
The phrase 'it is written' is not in the verse; the Book of Life image echoes earlier biblical ideas but this verse points to no specific OT passage, and no candidate matches.
The 'Book of Life' with names written in it is the concept of Ps 69:28 (blotted out of the Book of Life), the only candidate with the Book of Life.
The warning not to add to or take from God's words follows the OT formula of Deut 4:2 (and 12:32), not the book-finding narratives listed.
Same addition/removal warning, whose OT antecedent is Deut 4:2 (cf. Deut 12:32), not the candidates about written records.
John's vision of the scroll at the throne describes his own apocalyptic vision; it does not cite an OT passage, though it echoes throne visions like 1Kgs 22:19 (candidate 2).
The 'rest a little while longer' is apocalyptic narrative, not a citation of any OT passage; no candidate matches.
Rom 11:8 conflates Deut 29:4 ('eyes to see, ears to hear ... to this day') with Isa 29:10, and candidate 1 is that Deut 29:4 text.
The 'just as ... so' is Paul's own Adam/Christ comparison, not a citation of any OT verse; none of the candidates match.
Paul's 'type' is Adam in the Genesis 3 transgression narrative itself, not any listed candidate verse.
The 'disobedience of the one man' points to Adam's disobedience in Genesis 3, absent from the listed candidates.
Paul's own 'just as ... so' rhetorical parallel between sin reigning in death and grace reigning through righteousness; no OT passage is being cited or compared.
The 'type' label attaches to the passage's slavery/obedience imagery, which is Paul's own figure, not an OT citation; none of the six candidates is echoed.
Paul explicitly frames this as 'speaking in human terms'—his own analogy about offering members as slaves—not a citation of an OT text.
'Just as Christ was raised ... so we too' is Paul's analogy between Christ's resurrection and the believer's new walk, not a citation of an OT verse.
The 'fulfilled' here is the law's righteous requirement being met in believers by the Spirit, not an assertion that a specific OT prophecy is fulfilled; the candidates are irrelevant.

Paul's 'show yourself an example' is general parametric instruction, and the only plausible antecedent for 'a type' (Gk typos) of a blameless exemplar is the Ezekiel 28:12 lament over the king of Tyre (LXX: 'you are a seal of likeness/typos'); the six word-search candidates match only trivial words like 'works/hands/do' and plainly are not what Titus 2:7 cites.
